name: Treaty with the Seminole, 1832 (Treaty of Payne's Landing)
promises: The treaty was to bind only if a Seminole delegation, sent west at US expense, was satisfied with the land among the Creeks and with the Creeks' willingness to reunite with the Seminole as one people (preamble).
$15,400 for improvements given up in Florida, divided among chiefs and warriors by town and paid on arrival in the west.
An annuity of $3,000 a year for fifteen years once the whole tribe had removed, and the blacksmith annuity extended by ten years.
The United States would pay the cost of removal and supply food for up to twelve months after arrival, plus a blanket and frock for each person.
The United States would investigate claims for stolen or destroyed property and pay verified claims up to $7,000.

breaches.what: The Seminole of Florida (Docket 73) and the Seminole Nation of Oklahoma (Docket 151) claimed before the Indian Claims Commission for the 1823 cession and for the reservation ceded under this treaty. In 1970 the Commission found the 5,865,600-acre reservation worth $2,050,000 as of May 9, 1832, against $2,094,809.39 paid, held that payment not unconscionable and allowed nothing for it. The dockets were later settled by a $16,000,000 compromise in 1976. Neither is a finding that this treaty was broken.

breaches.what: Guy Osceola, spokesman for the Traditional Seminoles, told the Senate that the Traditional people were never heard by the Indian Claims Commission, were not consulted on the $16 million award covering the lands taken under this treaty and the 1823 treaty, and would not accept money for their land.

source.title: Distribution of Seminole Judgment Funds, Senate Select Committee on Indian Affairs hearing, March 2, 1978

breaches.quote: We feel that any bill that is passed that is allocated money to us we will not accept any kind of money.

compensation: In 1970 the Indian Claims Commission found the Seminole reservation ceded under this treaty was 5,865,600 acres worth $2,050,000 as of May 9, 1832, and that the $2,094,809.39 paid was not unconscionable (23 Ind. Cl. Comm. 108, 115). On 27 April 1976 the Commission approved a $16,000,000 compromise of all claims in Dockets 73 and 151, which covered the aboriginal lands ceded under the Treaty of Camp Moultrie (1823), valued in 1970 on 23,892,626 acres, and the reservation lands ceded in 1832 (38 Ind. Cl. Comm. 62). The money was divided by Public Law 101-277 in 1990 (Kersey summary).
today: The removal this treaty began was resisted in the Second Seminole War; Seminole communities remained in Florida and today are the Seminole Tribe of Florida and the Miccosukee Tribe, while the removed Seminole are the Seminole Nation of Oklahoma. Traditional Seminoles told the Senate in 1978 they would not accept money for their land.

nationVoice.summary: Their spokesman Guy Osceola told the Senate in 1978 that they had been denied a hearing for 28 years and would not accept money for land they still live on.
The tribe's museum publishes a summary of the land claims case, including the Florida petition's claim for land taken under Payne's Landing.

openQuestions: The condition precedent: the Fort Gibson agreement of 28 March 1833 (7 Stat. 423, proclaimed 12 April 1834, no Royce cession so not in the queue) records seven delegates as satisfied with the western land, and the United States treated that as making this treaty binding. Whether the delegates could bind the nation, or the nation in council had to decide, is the core dispute. John K. Mahon, 'Two Seminole Treaties' (Florida Historical Quarterly 41:1, 1962, stars.library.ucf.edu/fhq/vol41/iss1/5) addresses it but could not be loaded by a robot; Florida Memory's Payne's Landing and Fort Gibson lesson pages returned 403.

No court ruling, Act of Congress or government admission that this treaty specifically was breached was found; the ICC found the 1832 consideration not unconscionable. A deeper pass could check whether the removal subsistence, annuity and $7,000 property-claim promises were met.
The Seminole Nation of Oklahoma's own account of this treaty was not found online (sno-nsn.gov not reached).

Audit 2026-11-08: the Commission entry was sourced only to a museum summary of a history book; it now cites the Commission opinion and findings of May 13, 1970 and the 1976 compromise findings, all opened. The figures 5,865,600 acres, $2,050,000 and $2,094,809.39 (findings, p. 115 ff.) and the quote are confirmed; the opinion OCR misreads the payment as $2,094,603.33. The 4,032,940-acre figure for the 1950 petition, which came from the summary, was dropped. The compromise findings note that no recovery had been allowed for the 1832 reservation land. The 1976 award covered about 24 million acres of 1823 aboriginal land plus the 1832 reservation, so the earlier wording that put both treaties at about 24 million acres was narrowed.

plain.promised: The treaty was to bind only if a Seminole delegation was satisfied with land in the west. The United States promised payment for improvements, $3,000 a year for fifteen years, removal costs and up to a year of food.
plain.happened: No formal finding that this treaty was broken has been located. The Indian Claims Commission found in 1970 that the $2,094,809.39 paid for the reservation was not unconscionable. Traditional Seminoles told the Senate in 1978 they were never heard by the Commission.
plain.today: A $16,000,000 compromise in 1976 covered this and the 1823 treaty, and was divided by law in 1990. Seminole communities remained in Florida after resisting removal in the Second Seminole War.
